security_audit.summary: All 82 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown syntax, placeholder credentials, and legitimate Azure or loopback URLs. The skill contains no executable scripts, secret values, arbitrary command execution, or prompt injection. One medium semantic issue remains: a token-caching example actually enables account identifier logging and may expose identifiers.

remediation.issue: The token caching section enables account identifier logging, which can expose identifiers in application logs.
remediation.suggestion: Replace the example with documented cache configuration. Add a warning to enable account identifier logging only during controlled debugging with suitable privacy controls.

content.user_title: Configure Azure Identity Authentication in Java
content.value_statement: Java applications need secure authentication across local development, Azure hosting, pipelines, and interactive clients. This skill explains Azure Identity credentials, configuration patterns, and selection guidance.
actual_capabilities: Explain and configure DefaultAzureCredential for Azure SDK client builders.
Compare managed identity, service principal, certificate, browser, device code, CLI, and workload identity credentials.
Show Maven dependency coordinates for Azure Identity version 1.15.0.
Provide environment variable requirements for supported credential flows.
Demonstrate chained credentials, sovereign cloud authorities, token requests, logging, and error handling.
Recommend credentials for local, Azure-hosted, Kubernetes, CI/CD, desktop, and CLI environments.
limitations: Provides examples only and does not create app registrations, role assignments, or managed identities.
Does not validate tenant settings, redirect URIs, certificate permissions, or organization policies.
Uses Azure Identity version 1.15.0, so users must verify current compatibility and advisories.
Some examples use placeholders and require secure secret storage before production use.

use_cases.title: Secure an Azure-hosted service
use_cases.description: Select managed identity credentials and connect a Java backend to Azure services without stored application secrets.

use_cases.title: Configure pipeline authentication
use_cases.description: Choose environment or workload identity settings for Java builds that access Azure resources during automated delivery.

use_cases.title: Design interactive authentication
use_cases.description: Compare browser, device code, and Azure CLI credentials for desktop applications and command-line tools.

prompt_templates.title: Choose a credential
prompt_templates.prompt: My Java application runs in [environment] and accesses [Azure service]. Recommend an Azure Identity credential and explain the selection.

prompt_templates.title: Configure DefaultAzureCredential
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Java authentication plan using DefaultAzureCredential for [environment]. Include required setup, allowed credential sources, Azure client integration, and validation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Remove stored client secrets
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my Java service authentication approach and plan a migration from client secrets to [managed identity or workload identity]. Address permissions and deployment changes.

prompt_templates.title: Design multi-environment authentication
prompt_templates.prompt: Design Azure Identity authentication for local development, CI/CD, AKS, and production. Define credential precedence, tenant restrictions, sovereign-cloud support, logging controls, and failure handling.

output_examples.input: Which credential should a Java API on Azure App Service use for Blob Storage?
output: Recommendation: use the App Service managed identity through DefaultAzureCredential.
Access: assign only the required Blob Storage data role to that identity.
Validation: test token acquisition and storage authorization in the deployed environment.

output_examples.input: Plan migration of an AKS Java service from a client secret to workload identity.
output: Create a federated identity relationship for the Kubernetes service account.
Grant the identity the minimum Azure roles required by the service.
Configure workload identity variables and remove the stored client secret after validation.

output_examples.input: Help diagnose DefaultAzureCredential failures in local development.
output: Confirm Azure CLI login state and selected tenant.
Review excluded credential sources and application tenant restrictions.
Enable diagnostic logging temporarily, while keeping account identifiers and secrets protected.

best_practices: Use managed identity or workload identity in Azure-hosted production environments to avoid stored secrets.
Grant least privilege and verify tenant, role, endpoint, and redirect configuration for each environment.
Disable verbose and account identifier logging after debugging, and never place secrets in code or logs.
anti_patterns: Do not hardcode client secrets, passwords, certificate passwords, or tokens in Java source.
Do not use broad DefaultAzureCredential chains in production without reviewing allowed credential sources.
Do not enable account identifier or verbose logging in production without privacy and retention controls.

faq.question: Does this skill authenticate to Azure for me?
faq.answer: No. It provides Java guidance and examples. You must configure Azure identities, permissions, endpoints, and runtime settings.

faq.question: Which credential should most applications start with?
faq.answer: DefaultAzureCredential is useful across environments. Production deployments should restrict its sources or use a specific managed identity credential.

faq.question: Can I use the examples without Azure CLI?
faq.answer: Yes. Managed identity, workload identity, environment, certificate, browser, and device code credentials support other environments and application types.

faq.question: Does the skill support sovereign Azure clouds?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows authority host selection for Azure Government and Azure China.

faq.question: Does the skill store or rotate secrets?
faq.answer: No. Use managed identity when possible or an approved secret manager and rotation process.

faq.question: Is the listed dependency version always current?
faq.answer: No. The example uses Azure Identity 1.15.0. Verify the latest compatible release and security advisories before adoption.
